topic: Property Law: General Principles of Transfer of Property
description: This module introduces the foundational concepts of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (TPA). It covers the distinction between movable and immovable property, the rules governing what can and cannot be legally transferred, and key equitable doctrines such as Lis Pendens and Part Performance.

scope_and_types_of_property.concept: Scope of TPA: Inter Vivos Transfers & Types of Property
key_points: Inter Vivos: The Transfer of Property Act primarily governs transfers 'inter vivos'—meaning transfers between living persons (individuals or companies). It does not generally cover transfers by operation of law (like inheritance or insolvency) or by Will.

Immovable Property: TPA largely deals with immovable property. The Act defines it negatively: it 'does not include standing timber, growing crops, or grass'. Generally, it includes land, benefits arising out of land (like rent rights), and things attached to the earth (like buildings).
Movable Property: Governed primarily by the Sale of Goods Act, 1930, though the TPA contains some specific provisions for movable property (like gifts of movables).
The General Rule: Property of any kind may be transferred, except as specifically prohibited by the Act or any other law.

Spes Successionis: The chance of an heir-apparent succeeding to an estate, or the chance of a relation obtaining a legacy on the death of a kinsman, cannot be transferred. It is a mere expectation, not a present right.

Mere Right to Sue: A mere right to sue (e.g., a claim for unliquidated damages in a tort case) cannot be transferred. However, a right to recover a definite sum of money (actionable claim) can be transferred.

Other Exceptions: Public offices, the salary of a public officer (before or after it becomes payable), and rights strictly personal in nature (like a right to future maintenance) cannot be transferred.

key_doctrines.concept: Key Equitable Doctrines (Lis Pendens & Part Performance)
key_points: Doctrine of Lis Pendens (Section 52): 'Lis Pendens' means a pending suit. If a lawsuit regarding the title of an immovable property is pending in a competent court, the property cannot be transferred by any party to the suit so as to affect the rights of the opponent. The buyer takes the property subject to the final court decision.

Doctrine of Part Performance (Section 53A): Protects a buyer (transferee) who has taken possession of the property and performed their part of the contract (like paying the price), even if the legal transfer deed has not been formally registered. The seller cannot evict them merely on the ground of non-registration.

mcq_bank.subtopic: Scope of Transfer of Property Act

questions.question: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 primarily governs transfers of property that occur:

options.A: By operation of law, such as inheritance.
options.D: By orders of a criminal court.

questions.explanation: Section 5 of the TPA defines 'transfer of property' as an act by which a living person conveys property, in present or in future, to one or more other living persons. Thus, it primarily deals with 'inter vivos' transfers.

questions.question: Aman's father is a very wealthy man. Aman, hoping to inherit his father's vast estate after his death, 'sells' his expected future share of the inheritance to a money-lender today for cash. Under the Transfer of Property Act, is this transfer valid?

options.A: Yes, it is valid because property of any kind can be transferred.
options.B: Yes, provided the father gives a written consent.
options.C: No, it is void because it is a transfer of 'Spes Successionis' (a mere chance of inheritance), which cannot be transferred.
options.D: No, because a son cannot enter into a contract with a money-lender.

questions.explanation: Under Section 6(a) of the TPA, the chance of an heir-apparent succeeding to an estate ('Spes Successionis') is merely an expectation, not a vested legal right. Therefore, it cannot be legally transferred.

questions.question: Ravi and Suresh are engaged in a bitter legal battle in the High Court over the ownership of a commercial building. While the court case is still pending, Ravi secretly sells the building to an innocent third party, Vikram. When the court finally rules that Suresh is the true owner, what happens to Vikram's purchase?

options.A: Vikram gets to keep the property because he was an innocent buyer who paid in good faith.
options.B: The transfer to Vikram is completely null and void from the very beginning.
options.C: Vikram's purchase is subject to the court's decree under the Doctrine of Lis Pendens; therefore, he loses the property to Suresh.
options.D: Suresh and Vikram must divide the property equally.

questions.explanation: Under the Doctrine of Lis Pendens (Section 52), any transfer of property made during the pendency of a suit regarding that property's title is subject to the final outcome of the court case. Vikram cannot claim better rights than Ravi, and must surrender the property to the true owner (Suresh) as declared by the court.
